title: Krishna alone by the river
hookLine: Krishna sits alone by the Yamuna, and the god of the poem admits he let her walk away
carry: in bhakti, god longs for us too
last: RADHA AT THE EDGE OF THE DANCE.

cards: Krishna is sitting by the river Yamuna, alone, and he is not doing well. A little while ago he was at the center of a spring dance in the forest, everyone around him. Then he noticed someone missing.
Radha had seen him there, surrounded, and had quietly gone. He left the dance and searched the thickets and the vine bowers. Nothing.
Now he has sat down on the bank, and Jayadeva lets us listen while he talks to himself. It isn't the speech a listener might expect from a god.

teach.h: I DIDN'T STOP HER. I WAS AFRAID.
teach.b: Here is his song, in paraphrase. She saw me surrounded by the other women, and she walked away. I didn't stop her.
I was afraid, because I knew I was in the wrong. Then the refrain, again and again: Hari, Hari, through my own carelessness she has gone, angry, it seems.

teach.h: WHAT WILL SHE SAY TO ME?
teach.b: What will she do now? What will she say to me, after I've been away so long? What good is wealth, or people, or a home, without her?
He sees her face in his mind, the eyebrows drawn together in anger, and speaks to her as if she were there: forgive me, I won't do it again, let me see you.
This is the Lord of the poem, the one the opening hymn praised in every one of his descents into the world. And here he sits, admitting a mistake. How do devotees hold this?
In Vaishnava traditions, one answer is the word lila, play.

teach.h: LILA: LOVE IN ITS WHOLE RANGE.
teach.b: The divine takes on a lover's part fully, faults and all, so that love can be shown in its whole range: delight, hurt, regret, longing. It's easy to picture bhakti running one way, the soul reaching up toward God.
Here it runs the other way too.

teach.h: GOD IS THE ONE WHO MISSES.
teach.b: God is the one who misses, rehearsing an apology by the river.
For a devotee, that changes prayer: you aren't only reaching for God; on this reading, God is already looking for you. And Jayadeva closes his songs by naming himself, offering what he has sung.

how: Singers in Vaishnava communities perform the Gita Govinda's songs in temples and in concert, often one song at a time, and dancers in classical forms such as Odissi act out scenes like Krishna's lament by the river.

o: a strict duty of ritual owed to the family god
careful study of the sacred texts in Sanskrit
devotion, loving attention that here runs both ways

games.q: Krishna by the river — tap the pairs.
p: he was afraid, knowing his fault
play: love shown in its whole range
Jayadeva names himself in the song

s: in this passage, Radha is the only one who longs
Krishna searches for her, then sits by the Yamuna and laments that he let her go.
Krishna admits he was at fault
he says he didn't stop her because he was afraid, knowing he was in the wrong.
Jayadeva keeps himself out of his songs
he closes his songs by naming himself, offering what he has sung.

games.q: you're Krishna. the one you love has seen you with everyone else and walked away. what do you do?
o: go looking for her, and grieve when you can't find her.
send someone to tell her she's overreacting.
games.why: he leaves the dance, searches the thickets, then sits by the river and admits it was his fault.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've let walk away without a word: a friend you stopped calling, a small hurt you saw and didn't answer.

Don't fix anything; just sit on the riverbank with it, the way Krishna does in the poem, and let yourself see their face. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if you don't, simply stay with the memory, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. Devotion, loving attention. In the Gita Govinda it runs both ways: today, the one who longs is Krishna.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: lila, play. Vaishnava traditions use it for the divine taking part in the world freely, as in Krishna's love story.

carryVoice: Your line: in bhakti, God longs for us too. The longing runs both ways. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Gita Govinda, the canto of Krishna's remorse (Madhava by the Yamuna)
